title: House of Flying Daggers
full_review:
A lawman assigned to thwart a growing rebellion finds himself ensnared in a tangled web of desire, deception and betrayal in the sweeping and visually sumptuous martial arts love story "House of Flying Daggers" (Sony Pictures Classics).

Part sword spectacle, part triangular romance, director Zhang Yimou's kung fu saga echoes the cinematic bravura of Ang Lee's "Crouching Tiger, Hidden Dragon," as well as Yimou's own Oscar-nominated "Hero" and explores universal themes of passion, jealousy, vengeance and the timeless conflict between love and duty.

"House of Flying Daggers" takes place in ninth-century China, as the sun sets on the once flourishing Tang Dynasty. The flagging government is threatened by shadowy insurgent armies -- including the titular blade-flinging fraternity -- formed to protest imperial court corruption and challenge the emperor's waning power. With the anti-government forces gaining momentum, two high-ranking members of the imperial constabulary -- Jin (Takeshi Kaneshiro) and his captain, Leo (Andy Lau), devise a plot to squelch the rebels' efforts by capturing their elusive leader.

Acting on information that a beautiful blind courtesan, Mei (Ziyi Zhang), has ties to the guerrilla group, Jin, posing as a moneyed playboy, is dispatched to the brothel where Mei dances. After an electrifying set piece based on a traditional dance called "The Echo Game," Mei is arrested and imprisoned by Leo. Jin fakes a jailbreak and offers to escort Mei (who can also wield a mean sword) back to the Robin Hood-like rebels' secret base, feigning sympathy for their cause. Jin, assuming the name Wind, surreptitiously marks their trail, making it easy for Leo -- and a small contingent of imperial troops -- to track their movements.

Even a sightless strumpet can see what will happen next. Jin and Mei fall in love, setting up the tale's conflict-of-interests conundrum. Plot twists abound. Trusts are broken, loyalties questioned, hidden motives disclosed, true identities revealed and hearts are pierced by flying daggers (literally and figuratively).

With the porcelain beauty of a china doll, Zhang is breathtaking to watch, whether exchanging demure glances with Kaneshiro or kicking Tang "tuchis." Kaneshiro strikes the perfect balance between roguish charm and chivalric virtue. Together they generate quite a bit of heavy panting, including an impassioned love scene in a field of tall grass.

Unfortunately, the story sometimes gets drowned out by the swirl of steel and silk. However, the characters and their dilemmas d'amour are interesting enough to keep viewers engaged in the story during breaks in the eye-popping action.

And while "House of Flying Daggers" lacks the emotional intimacy of Yimou's more quietly poetic dramas like "Raise the Red Lantern" and the epic scope of "Hero" (not to mention the latter's almost symphonic use of color), the gravity-defying fight sequences -- elegantly choreographed by Tony Ching Siu-Tung -- are nothing short of spectacular.

The film's centerpiece is a dazzling blade ballet which takes place in and above a mist-shrouded bamboo grove between the star-crossed lovers and the emperor's death squad (enhanced, as are all the battles, by some computer generated effects). Viewers sensitive to violence should be aware that, though artfully done, the clashes contain shots of the thrown knives slicing the throats of their intended targets.

The film's melodramatic tone crescendos to operatic heights during the picture's climactic duel in the snow (all that's missing is the "O Fortuna" chorus from Carl Orff's "Carmina Burana").

Still, if you are tired of cookie-cutter action movies and are looking for something that is artistic as well as exciting, "House of Flying Daggers" hits the mark.

Subtitles.

Because of much stylized action violence and associated gore, attempted rape and a sexual encounter, the USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-III -- adults. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG-13 -- parents are strongly cautioned. Some material may be inappropriate for children under 13.
